messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For Raj, the memory of that night was not so much a story he told himself as something that happened to him without warning. His ex-girlfriend’s accusations had escalated fast; she had been sweating, her body odour sharp with anger, and when she started hitting him, he had frozen. He never hit back, never even raised his hands to defend himself. In the months and years that followed, he could not forgive himself for that. The rage he felt when he remembered—sometimes his fists would clench without any clear image, just a wave of hot fury—made him feel like a stranger to his own body. And his body kept reacting as if the danger were still present, his heart pounding, his muscles tensing, even when he was alone in his shop at night.

He owned a small convenience store in a suburban strip mall, and his days were punctuated by the smells and sounds of customers. It was a whiff of sweat—a labourer coming in after work, a teenager after a run—that would do it first: the memory would surge up without warning, and he would feel the same helpless rage. Certain conversation topics, especially anyone raising their voice in an argument, could also send him spiralling. He began to dread the evening shift most of all. As dusk fell, every stranger who walked through the door felt like a potential threat. He found himself scanning faces, watching hands, his body bracing. That hypervigilance made him notice triggers more—the smell of sweat seemed to linger everywhere, and any raised voice was amplified. He had trouble falling asleep at night, lying awake listening for sounds, convinced he was not safe even in his own bedroom.

The guilt was the worst part. He would replay that night over and over, telling himself he should have done something—called the police, pushed her away, anything. That belief that he could not rely on himself had seeped into every part of his life. Now, when a stranger approached him too quickly in the store, his first thought was not that he was safe but that he would freeze again. This made the threat feel overwhelming, and that feeling of threat, in turn, made him more attuned to triggers; he would catch the scent of sweat and his stomach would drop, knowing the image was about to hit. The memory itself fed the guilt: as soon as he remembered the event, he was flooded with self-blame. And his belief that his body was an enemy—that it kept reacting to safety as if it were danger—meant that ordinary triggers like a particular conversation topic could instantly revive the memory, because his body would respond first, and the image would follow. Each time a scent or topic brought the memory back, he felt a fresh wave of self-blame, confirming that he could not rely on himself. The memory left him raw and alert, so that the next smell or raised voice hit even harder.

By the time Raj finally came to the clinic, his relationship with his current partner was strained. He had started avoiding going out at night, and she did not understand why the smell of her cooking—something about the steam and salt—could make him withdraw. What frightened him most was the feeling that he was still the same person who had frozen that night, that nothing had changed. He hoped that talking about it would somehow loosen the grip of the memories, but he was terrified that the therapist would confirm what he already believed: that he had failed himself, and that he could never be safe again.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals directly lead to increased sensitivity or noticing of triggers; instead, threat leads to triggers, and negative appraisals lead to threat or memory.
